meta: Gravelot's 1720 design for the ornamental border around the general chart in John Pine's Tapestry Hangings in the House of Lords.
about: Britannia sits at the upper right with a sword and shield, ready to vanquish three figures below her. They are Envy, a bare-breasted woman holding a snake, Superstition, a blindfolded figure with a torch, and Spain, a fallen man with a sword beside a tower and a lion. At the top centre of the scrollwork border is a diadem made of ship prows. At the bottom is the head of Neptune with some of his attributes. The central shape and four unfinished circles in the corners, meant for globes, are cut out.

meta: Jan van Huysum's Flowers in an Urn, painted around 1720, signed on the marble tabletop and bought by the National Gallery of Art in 1977.
about: A bouquet of tulips, poppies, irises, roses and carnations spills from a terracotta urn carved with putti. A butterfly rests among the blooms, and a small bird's nest with pale blue eggs sits nearby. Jan van Huysum signed it on the front of the marble table. The dealer Jacques Goudstikker of Amsterdam owned it by 1919. Lord Claud Hamilton acquired it in 1924 through the London dealers Leggatt Brothers, and after a sale of his widow's property in 1975 the museum bought it.

meta: Michel Lasne's 1630 engraving of the Virgin and Child in the clouds above Saint Anthony.
about: The Virgin and Child sit in the clouds at upper left with four putti. Below, under a tree, Saint Anthony looks up at them, and a book lies open at his right. A Latin verse runs beneath the picture. It gives thanks to the saint for victory over an enemy and says the victory belongs to the Virgin's milk and her Son's blood. The names of the artists and the date follow the verse.

meta: Jasper Francis Cropsey's 1851 painting of Tourn Mountain in Rockland County, bought by William Wilson Corcoran and listed as Washington's Headquarters.
about: A wooded mountain rises above a dark river, with a small white cottage with a red roof in a sunlit meadow at left. Warm clouds catch the late light. Jasper Francis Cropsey dated it 1851 and lent it to an exhibition in Boston two years later. William Wilson Corcoran bought it from the artist by 1857, although the artist's account book records no sale. Corcoran's catalogue called it Washington's Headquarters on the Hudson River. He gave it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art in 1869.
credit_line: Corcoran Collection (Gift of William Wilson Corcoran, 1869)

meta: Jan Gossaert's grisaille panel of Saint Jerome Penitent, with a false Dürer monogram on a small stone.
about: A gaunt, bare-chested old man kneels in a rocky wilderness, gazing upward and striking his breast. A lion crouches beside him and a cardinal's hat lies at his feet. Behind him are a Gothic church and towers. The monogram AD on a small stone at center right is false. Jan Gossaert painted the panel around 1510. John M. Romadka owned it in Prague and Milwaukee by 1858, and the dealer Duveen had it by 1945. The Kress Foundation bought it in 1949.
dimensions:
painted surface: 86.7 x 24.5 cm (34 1/8 x 9 5/8 in.)
overall (panel): 86.7 x 25.3 cm (34 1/8 x 9 15/16 in.)
framed: 94.3 x 61.2 x 5.7 cm (37 1/8 x 24 1/8 x 2 1/4 in.)

meta: Rembrandt Peale's 1802 portrait of Timothy Matlack writing at a desk, owned by his great-granddaughter and lent to a Philadelphia society.
about: An older man with dark, wavy hair sits at a desk in a tan coat, writing with a quill on a sheet of paper. A folded letter rests nearby. The sitter is Timothy Matlack. Rembrandt Peale painted him in 1802. His great-granddaughter, Martha Whitney, deposited the portrait at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania in 1872. In 1923 it was sold to the collector Thomas B. Clarke. The Mellon Trust bought it in 1936 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1947.

meta: Michael Sweerts's 1646 painting of the hungry being fed, one of a series on the seven works of mercy.
about: A crowd of ragged poor people gathers on the steps of a church in an Italian setting to be fed. At the centre a beggar stands leaning on a wooden stick. Michael Sweerts painted the scene in 1646. The Rijksmuseum has it as one of a series of paintings of the seven works of mercy. Look for the man at the centre with his stick.

meta: Nicolas Lancret's Picnic after the Hunt, once in the palaces of Frederick the Great and later owned by Kaiser Wilhelm II.
about: Elegantly dressed figures in silk and brocade gather beneath a large spreading tree after a hunt, with horses and hunting dogs nearby. Open countryside with distant hills and a village stretches into a bright sky. Nicolas Lancret painted it around 1735 to 1740. Frederick II, King of Prussia, owned it at Potsdam, and a description of his palaces from 1773 lists it. It stayed in the Hohenzollern family until Kaiser Wilhelm II. Wildenstein bought it in 1923, and the Kress Foundation acquired it in 1946.

meta: Giovanni Bellini's Portrait of a Young Man in Red, painted around 1480, possibly listed in Andrea Vendramin's Venice collection in 1627.
about: A young man in a red garment with a white collar wears a dark hood draped over his shoulders and head. He is turned three-quarters to the left against a blue sky with soft clouds. The art historian Tancred Borenius suggested that the portrait may be the picture attributed to Bellini in a 1627 inventory of Andrea Vendramin's collection in Venice. Count Manfred von Ingenheim later owned it. Andrew W. Mellon bought it through Duveen in 1930, and it came to the National Gallery of Art in 1937.

meta: Giovanni Battista Foggini's design for a wall decoration for Cosimo III de' Medici, centred on an armoured king on horseback.
about: An armoured king gallops to the left in the central field. He was to be made in high relief and to stand on a console in front of rose marble. The frame is metal with blue marble inside. At the top two winged putti sit on a volute. With their right hands they hold a blue ball bearing three golden lilies, and with their left hands they lift a royal crown. Giovanni Battista Foggini drew the design for Cosimo III de' Medici around 1700.

meta: Govaert Flinck's 1646 Portrait of a Woman, long thought to show the scholar Anna Maria van Schurman.
about: A woman in a black dress with a deep white lace collar fastened by a ribbon bow looks straight at the viewer against a dark background. An inscription on the back led people to think she was Anna Maria van Schurman, a prominent Dutch scholar and artist. The Cleveland Museum of Art says those words were added much later and give her age as 42, when Anna Maria would have been 39. The likeness also does not match other known portraits of her. Her identity remains unknown.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Noah L. Butkin

meta: Jean Joseph Benjamin-Constant's 1890 portrait of John Brooks Henderson, the Missouri senator who served as the first special prosecutor in US history.
about: An older bald man with a beard sits for the portrait in round pince-nez glasses, a dark overcoat and a green waistcoat, against a deep red ground. He is John Brooks Henderson, a lawyer by training who served in the Missouri House and then in the US Senate. Though he was himself an enslaver, he helped win ratification of the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. His vote against impeaching President Andrew Johnson ended his Senate career. In 1875 Ulysses S. Grant appointed him special prosecutor in the Whiskey Ring scandal.

meta: Frank Duveneck's portrait of the painter William Gedney Bunce, owned by a neighbour and a collector before the Mellon Trust.
about: A bearded man with reddish hair sits against a dark background in a dark jacket over a black vest with a white collar. He holds a cigar loosely in his clasped hands, and a watch chain crosses his front. The sitter was William Gedney Bunce. A neighbour of his, George Meyers, owned the portrait, and Alfred M. Turner then had it from around 1894. In 1919 Turner sold it to the collector Thomas B. Clarke. The Mellon Trust bought it in 1936 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1942.

meta: Edmund Blair Leighton's A Wet Sunday Morning, a Regency scene of a young man walking a young woman home under an umbrella.
about: A young man in a tan riding coat and cream breeches walks a young woman home under a pale umbrella along a rain-slicked village lane. She wears a pink bodice and a white dress. Two other young women look on with interest from the church porch. Wikimedia Commons describes the painting as a genre scene of the early nineteenth century, the period known as the Regency. Edmund Blair Leighton painted it. Look at the onlookers in the porch.

meta: Cornelis van Poelenburch's Italianate landscape, which the Rijksmuseum reads as Jesse presenting his youngest son David to the prophet Samuel.
about: A wide landscape of hills with buildings has herdsmen and cattle at either side. In the middle three main figures stand before a flock of sheep. The Rijksmuseum reads the scene as Jesse introducing his youngest son David to the prophet Samuel, from the First Book of Samuel, chapter 16. The sheep are the flock David had been tending. Cornelis van Poelenburch signed it on a rock at lower left with the monogram C P F. The title still calls the subject unidentified.

meta: Pieter Jansz Quast's 1635 painting of two card players and a woman smoking a pipe, bought by the Rijksmuseum at a Leiden sale in 1885.
about: Two men stand absorbed in a card game at a wooden table, with a third peering from behind. A seated woman in an embroidered gold gown holds a pipe and glances toward the viewer. Pieter Jansz Quast signed the picture with a ligature of his initials. It was sold at the C.F. Berré sale in Leiden in 1885 as a work by J. Uchtervelt. The museum bought it there for either 147 or 171 guilders.

meta: Henri Edmond Cross's Beach at Cabasson, painted in 1891 and 1892 after he moved to the Côte d'Azur because of rheumatoid arthritis.
about: Three boys in light swimwear rest and stand on pale sand beside a rust-colored rocky outcrop. A windswept pine branch reaches in from the right, and calm blue water stretches beyond. In 1891 Henri Edmond Cross moved to Cabasson, a hamlet on the Côte d'Azur, because of his rheumatoid arthritis. The Art Institute of Chicago says the move deeply affected his art. He adopted divided brushwork, small dashes and dots of color, and used it systematically to convey the color and heat of the region.
credit_line: L. L. and A. S. Coburn, and Bette and Neison Harris funds; Charles H. and Mary F. S. Worcester Collection; through prior acquisition of the Kate L. Brewster Collection

meta: Jean-Étienne Liotard's 1764 pastel Madame de Vermenoux Pays Homage to Apollo, his largest pastel on parchment.
about: A woman in a white satin gown with a blue sash and pearl trim reaches toward a marble bust of Apollo. The bust stands on a pedestal carved with a serpent, and its inscription reads NAMQ ERIT ILLE MIHI SEMP DEUS. Jean-Étienne Liotard made the portrait in pastel on parchment. The Staatliche Kunsthalle Karlsruhe counts him among the leading pastel painters of the Rococo and calls this one of his most notable portraits. It is also the largest pastel he made on parchment.

meta: Adriaen Pietersz van de Venne's 1642 allegory of the stadtholdership of Prince Frederick Henry, with Victory handing him a laurel wreath.
about: Winged putti fly through a golden, cloud-filled sky with a crown and laurel wreaths. Below them Victoria, the female personification of victory, holds a palm branch and hands the stadtholder a laurel wreath. Between them stands Willem II, looking on. A servant holds the reins of a saddled horse, and a dog waits in the foreground. Adriaen Pietersz van de Venne signed and dated the allegory in 1642. The Stedelijk Museum Het Prinsenhof lends it to the Rijksmuseum.

meta: Fra Angelico's The Healing of Palladia, painted around 1438 for the high altar of San Marco in Florence.
about: Two episodes share the panel. On the left, two haloed saints tend a woman lying in bed while attendants watch. On the right, a haloed saint receives a small object from a woman in a doorway. The painting stood on the high altar of the church of San Marco in Florence from about 1440 until about 1677. Later records place it in the convent's pharmacy, and by 1841 it belonged to the comte de Pourtalès-Gorgier in Paris. His sale in 1865 listed it as by Masaccio.

meta: Bronzino's Portrait of a Woman, painted around 1550, an unidentified sitter probably linked to the Medici court.
about: Bronzino was court painter to Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence. The woman in this portrait cannot be definitively identified, but the Cleveland Museum of Art thinks she was probably connected to the Medici court. It says Bronzino stresses wealth, status and courtly refinement over personality. The plain background adds monumentality despite the small size. Her hand rests on her chest with the fingers spread, a gesture that goes back to an ancient Greek pose of modesty.

meta: Meindert Hobbema's Wooded Landscape with Figures, painted around 1658 and acquired by the National Gallery of Art in 2015.
about: A dirt track curves through a grove of tall trees in autumn color, where two figures walk with a dog toward the viewer. Towering clouds fill the sky above a flat plain. Meindert Hobbema signed with a monogram at lower right. The London collector Sir George Donaldson owned the painting, and William A. Clark bought it in 1906. Clark left it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art in 1926, and it passed to the National Gallery of Art in 2015.

meta: Jean-Charles Delafosse's 1760 design for a decorative ewer with a swan, a harpy and a satyr on the handle.
about: The handle of this ewer is a swan kissing a harpy, who is encircled by a crouching female satyr. The body is decorated in neoclassical style, with fluting, rope-like festoons, a female mask and suspended garlands of fruit. Coiled snakes form the base. Jean-Charles Delafosse drew the design in pen and grey wash.

meta: Henry Inman's portrait of the actor James Henry Hackett in the character of Rip Van Winkle.
about: An elderly bearded man in a rust-brown costume with a black belt stands on a forest path, gazing upward and extending one arm toward the branches. A distant lake and hills open through the trees on the left. The actor is James Henry Hackett, who was born in New York City in 1800. The National Portrait Gallery calls him a character actor who specialized in comic types. He made his theatrical debut in 1826 and was among the first performers to turn success in the United States into triumph on the British stage.
